title: Nataraja and the dance in the pine forest
hookLine: proud sages send a tiger, a snake and a dwarf against a wandering beggar, and he dances
tomorrow: why would a hymn bow to Shiva's anger?

lines: A TIGER: HE WEARS ITS SKIN.
A SNAKE: HE WEARS IT AS A GARLAND.
A DWARF: HE DANCES ON HIM.
cards: A wandering beggar walks into a pine forest where proud sages live, and they don't recognize him. In the Tamil temple tradition of Chidambaram, the beggar is Shiva.
The sages, furious, light a fire to destroy him and send a tiger out of it. He peels off its skin and wraps it round his waist. They send a snake.
He hangs it round his neck like a garland. They send a snarling dwarf, and Shiva sets one foot on the dwarf's back, lifts the other, and dances. The sages fall silent, and bow.
Today's summit sit goes back to that dance: Nataraja, the lord of the dance.

teach.h: THE DRUM AND THE FLAME, LEVEL.
teach.b: The bronze you've seen in a museum freezes that moment. Read it now all at once. In one hand, a small drum: the sound of things beginning.
In the hand across from it, a flame: the ending, held level with the drum.

teach.h: A RAISED HAND: DO NOT FEAR.
teach.b: Another hand is raised, palm out: do not fear.
Under the planted foot lies the dwarf from the forest, named Apasmara, forgetfulness, held down but never killed.
Tamil Shaiva teaching reads the whole figure as Shiva's five acts in the world: making, keeping, ending, concealing, and grace. And here's the heart of it.

teach.h: THE HAND POINTS TO THE LIFTED FOOT.
teach.b: One arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and its hand points down to the lifted foot. That foot is grace, the refuge.
The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang, in paraphrase, that just to see that lifted foot would make a human birth worth having.
So the teaching isn't only that beginnings and endings dance together, though they do: the drum doesn't wait for the flame. It's that inside all the turning, the god himself points to the way out.
That's why a Bharatanatyam dancer salutes Nataraja before she begins: her dance is offered into his. And it's how a Shaiva meets a crowded week.
A newborn and a goodbye, a new job and an ending: the drum and the flame aren't yours to balance. They're in his hands. Your part is to look where his hand points.

how: Nataraja is worshiped in temples and homes, notably at Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu, and the figure is honored in classical dance, where dancers often begin by saluting him.

o: a bronze kept locked in a museum's glass case
a temple dance performed only on festival nights
Shiva's dance: five acts at once, and the lifted foot as grace

games.q: the dancer, read whole — tap the pairs.
p: the ending, held level with the drum

s: Nataraja's drum and flame show creation first, then destruction later
they're held level in the same moment: the beginning and the ending together.
the dwarf under the foot is crushed to death
Apasmara, forgetfulness, is held down, never killed.
Tamil Shaiva teaching reads the dance as making, keeping, ending, concealing and grace
Shiva's five acts, all in one moment.

games.q: you're one of the pine-forest sages. you sent a tiger, a snake and a dwarf, and the beggar is dancing on the dwarf. one of his hands points down. where should you look?
o: at the fire you lit; it's coming for you.
at the lifted foot: that's grace, the way out.
nowhere; the hand is just there for balance.
games.why: the elephant-trunk hand points to the lifted foot, which Tamil Shaiva teaching reads as grace: the refuge in the middle of the dance.

practice: Notice that each breath is already ending as it begins, the in-breath turning, the out-breath turning.
Then let the week come to mind all at once, not in order: something that began, something that ended, something you feared, held together like the drum and the flame.
If you pray, rest before Shiva, the dancer, with all of it, and say softly, om namah shivaya. If you don't, simply let it all be held for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch: Nataraja, read all at once, with the hand that points to the lifted foot. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: naṭarāja, the lord of the dance, Shiva dancing in the ring of fire.

carryVoice: Your line: shiva's lifted foot is grace. The drum and the flame held level, and a hand pointing the way. A week closes here.

sources.ref: Koyil Puranam (Chidambaram tradition): Shiva in the Taruka (pine) forest; the tiger, the serpent and the dwarf sent by the sages; the dance
Nataraja iconography as read in Tamil Shaiva tradition: the five acts (pancakritya); the lifted foot as grace (e.g., Unmai Vilakkam on the dance)
Appar, Tevaram (fourth Tirumurai): the verse on seeing the dancer's lifted foot at Chidambaram
